206_bones_support_protection_movement_: 206 bones — support, protection, movement, mineral storage, hematopoiesis.
houses_meninges_brain_and_cranial_nerv: Houses meninges, brain, and cranial nerve foramina. Sutures (coronal, sagittal, lambdoid) fuse by age 2.
600_muscles_movement_posture_heat_prod: 600+ muscles — movement, posture, heat production, joint stabilization.
heart_60_000_miles_of_vessels_5l_of_bl: Heart, 60,000 miles of vessels, 5L of blood — delivers O₂, nutrients, hormones; removes waste.
cns_brain_spinal_cord_and_pns_31_spina: CNS (brain + spinal cord) and PNS (31 spinal nerve pairs, 12 cranial nerve pairs, autonomic NS).
lightest_sleep_transition_from_wakeful: Lightest sleep — transition from wakefulness. Slow rolling eye movements, muscle tone decreasing. Hypnic jerks (myoclonic twitches) common. Easily aroused. Vertex sharp waves appear on EEG.
true_sleep_begins_core_body_temperatur: True sleep begins. Core body temperature drops, heart rate slows. Sleep spindles (thalamocortical bursts) protect sleep and consolidate motor memory. K-complexes are large waveforms responding to external stimuli.
deep_slow_wave_sleep_sws_most_restorat: Deep/slow-wave sleep (SWS). Most restorative stage. Growth hormone secretion peaks. Glymphatic system clears brain waste (amyloid-β). Declarative memory consolidation occurs. Hardest to awaken from; sleep inertia if aroused.
dreaming_stage_brain_is_highly_active_: Dreaming stage. Brain is highly active (similar to waking) but body is paralyzed (atonia via brainstem inhibition of motor neurons). Rapid conjugate eye movements. Emotional memory processing and creative problem-solving. Cycles lengthen through the night.
brodmann_areas_map_52_cytoarchitectura: Brodmann areas map 52 cytoarchitectural regions. Primary motor cortex (area 4), primary somatosensory (areas 3,1,2), primary visual (area 17), primary auditory (areas 41,42). Prefrontal cortex is last to myelinate (age ~25).
purkinje_cells_are_among_the_largest_n: Purkinje cells are among the largest neurons, each receiving ~200,000 synaptic inputs. Cerebellar cortex has 3 layers: molecular, Purkinje, granular. Emerging research shows roles in cognition, emotion, and language.
contains_nuclei_for_cranial_nerves_iii: Contains nuclei for cranial nerves III–XII. Reticular activating system (RAS) is the brain's "on switch" — damage causes coma. Decussation of pyramids in medulla: motor crossover explains contralateral motor control.
memory_replay_during_sleep_hippocampal: Memory replay during sleep: hippocampal neurons "replay" daytime experiences during N3 sleep, transferring memories to neocortex. Grid cells in entorhinal cortex provide spatial coordinates to hippocampal place cells.
fear_conditioning_pathway_auditory_cor: Fear conditioning pathway: auditory cortex → lateral amygdala → central amygdala → hypothalamus (stress response) + PAG (freezing). Amygdala-prefrontal interactions allow emotional regulation — basis of CBT therapy.
key_nuclei_vpl_vpm_somatosensory_relay: Key nuclei: VPL/VPM (somatosensory relay), LGN (visual relay to V1), MGN (auditory relay to A1), pulvinar (attention), anterior nuclear group (memory, Papez circuit).
thermostat_analogy_anterior_hypothalam: Thermostat analogy: anterior hypothalamus triggers cooling (vasodilation, sweating); posterior hypothalamus triggers warming (shivering, vasoconstriction). Fever = elevated set point by prostaglandins from infection.
split_brain_experiments_revealed_hemis: Split-brain experiments revealed hemispheric specialization: left hemisphere = language, logic; right hemisphere = spatial, holistic processing. Information presented to one visual field is processed by contralateral hemisphere.
dopamine_from_substantia_nigra_modulat: Dopamine from substantia nigra modulates the direct (D1, excitatory) and indirect (D2, inhibitory) pathways. Loss of this modulation in Parkinson creates the characteristic difficulty initiating movement.
returns_interstitial_fluid_absorbs_die: Returns interstitial fluid, absorbs dietary fat, immune surveillance — 600–700 lymph nodes, thymus, spleen.
major_visceral_organs_respiration_dige: Major visceral organs — respiration, digestion, filtration, endocrine regulation.
skin_largest_organ_2m_hair_nails_gland: Skin (largest organ, ~2m²), hair, nails, glands — barrier, thermoregulation, sensation, vitamin D synthesis.
oxygen_delivery_and_co_removal_12_20_b: Oxygen delivery and CO₂ removal — ~12–20 breaths/min, ~6L air/min, 300 million alveoli.
hormone_producing_glands_regulate_meta: Hormone-producing glands — regulate metabolism, growth, reproduction, stress, homeostasis via chemical messengers.
male_and_female_reproductive_organs_ga: Male and female reproductive organs — gamete production, fertilization, fetal development, hormonal regulation.
the_circulatory_system_delivers_deoxyg: The circulatory system delivers deoxygenated blood to the lungs, where the respiratory system loads it with oxygen and offloads carbon dioxide across the thin alveolar-capillary membrane.
motor_neurons_from_the_nervous_system_: Motor neurons from the nervous system release acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, triggering muscle fiber contraction. Without neural signals, muscles cannot move.
muscles_attach_to_bones_via_tendons_an: Muscles attach to bones via tendons and pull across joints, creating lever systems. The skeleton provides rigid levers; muscles provide the pulling force.
the_hypothalamus_pituitary_axis_releas: The hypothalamus-pituitary axis releases FSH and LH that regulate the gonads. Estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone from reproductive organs feedback to the endocrine system.
the_lymphatic_system_returns_interstit: The lymphatic system returns interstitial fluid to the bloodstream and deploys immune cells made in lymphoid organs. Both systems maintain fluid homeostasis and fight infection.
the_hypothalamus_bridges_the_nervous_a: The hypothalamus bridges the nervous and endocrine systems — it integrates neural signals and translates them into hormonal commands that control the pituitary gland and all downstream hormone cascades.
the_diaphragm_and_intercostal_muscles_: The diaphragm and intercostal muscles physically expand and compress the thoracic cavity to move air. Lungs have no muscle themselves and rely entirely on surrounding muscles.
the_skin_contains_millions_of_speciali: The skin contains millions of specialized nerve endings and encapsulated receptors that detect touch, pressure, temperature, and pain, feeding constant sensory data to the nervous system.
blood_from_the_gi_tract_drains_through: Blood from the GI tract drains through the hepatic portal vein directly to the liver before entering general circulation, allowing the liver to process nutrients and detoxify substances first.
red_bone_marrow_inside_the_skeleton_is: Red bone marrow inside the skeleton is the birthplace of all blood cells. Red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets are all produced here through hematopoiesis.
which_structure_is_most_likely_affecte: Which structure is most likely affected?
patellofemoral_pain_syndrome_occurs_wh: Patellofemoral pain syndrome occurs when the patella does not track smoothly in its groove on the femur. Repeated stress from running causes cartilage irritation. Treatment includes quad strengthening, hip stabilization, and activity modification.
which_structure_is_most_likely_torn: Which structure is most likely torn?
the_supraspinatus_is_the_most_commonly: The supraspinatus is the most commonly torn rotator cuff muscle. It runs under the acromion where it is susceptible to impingement and tears. Overhead work like painting increases this risk significantly.
which_structure_controls_the_normal_he: Which structure controls the normal heart rhythm?
the_sa_node_in_the_right_atrium_is_the: The SA node in the right atrium is the heart's natural pacemaker. During intense exercise, adrenaline can cause benign palpitations as the heart rate adjusts. Persistent arrhythmias should be evaluated to rule out structural heart disease.
carpal_tunnel_syndrome_is_compression_: Carpal tunnel syndrome is compression of the median nerve under the flexor retinaculum at the wrist. The median nerve supplies sensation to the thumb and first 3.5 fingers. Repetitive wrist use is a major risk factor.
what_diagnosis_must_be_urgently_ruled_: What diagnosis must be urgently ruled out?
painless_lymphadenopathy_with_b_sympto: Painless lymphadenopathy with B-symptoms (night sweats, weight loss, fever) is the classic presentation of Hodgkin lymphoma in young adults. Biopsy showing Reed-Sternberg cells confirms the diagnosis.
which_cells_failed_and_what_is_the_eme: Which cells failed, and what is the emergency condition?
beta_cells_of_islets_of_langerhans_dia: Beta cells of islets of Langerhans; Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
without_insulin_from_beta_cells_glucos: Without insulin from beta cells, glucose cannot enter cells. The body burns fat, producing ketones that acidify the blood. Kussmaul breathing compensates by exhaling CO2. Treatment: IV fluids, insulin drip, and electrolyte replacement.
why_is_the_middle_third_of_the_clavicl: Why is the middle third of the clavicle the most common fracture site?
the_middle_third_is_thinnest_and_has_n: The middle third is thinnest and has no muscular reinforcement
the_clavicle_is_the_most_frequently_fr: The clavicle is the most frequently fractured bone. Its middle third is thinnest and lacks muscular protection. Force from a fall on an outstretched hand concentrates at this weak point. Most heal with sling immobilization.
why_does_altitude_cause_these_symptoms: Why does altitude cause these symptoms, and which structure is most stressed?
the_alveoli_and_respiratory_muscles_re: The alveoli and respiratory muscles; reduced atmospheric oxygen causes hypoxia
at_high_altitude_atmospheric_pressure_: At high altitude, atmospheric pressure drops, reducing the partial pressure of oxygen. Less oxygen crosses the alveolar membrane. The body compensates by breathing faster and deeper, increasing respiratory muscle work.
follow_a_red_blood_cell_through_the_en: Follow a red blood cell through the entire circulatory system.
deoxygenated_blood_from_the_body_enter: Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium via the superior and inferior vena cava.
blood_passes_through_the_tricuspid_val: Blood passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which pumps it toward the lungs.
the_right_ventricle_ejects_blood_throu: The right ventricle ejects blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary arteries toward both lungs.
in_the_alveolar_capillaries_co2_is_rel: In the alveolar capillaries, CO2 is released and O2 is picked up through the thin alveolar membrane.
freshly_oxygenated_blood_returns_to_th: Freshly oxygenated blood returns to the heart via the four pulmonary veins.
the_four_pulmonary_veins_empty_oxygena: The four pulmonary veins empty oxygenated blood into the left atrium, which fills and then pushes it through the mitral valve.
blood_passes_through_the_mitral_valve_: Blood passes through the mitral valve into the muscular left ventricle, the strongest heart chamber.
the_left_ventricle_powerfully_ejects_b: The left ventricle powerfully ejects blood through the aortic valve into the aorta, the body's main highway.
arteries_branch_into_arterioles_and_ca: Arteries branch into arterioles and capillaries where O2 and nutrients are delivered and CO2/waste collected.
deoxygenated_blood_returns_through_ven: Deoxygenated blood returns through venules and veins, assisted by muscle pumps and valves, back to the right atrium.
trace_the_journey_of_a_breath_of_air_f: Trace the journey of a breath of air from nose to alveoli and back.
air_enters_through_the_nostrils_and_is: Air enters through the nostrils and is warmed, humidified, and filtered by mucous membranes and turbinates.
air_passes_through_the_nasopharynx_and: Air passes through the nasopharynx and oropharynx, a shared passage with the digestive tract.
air_crosses_the_vocal_cords_in_the_voi: Air crosses the vocal cords in the voice box. The epiglottis guards against food entering the airway.
the_trachea_windpipe_is_reinforced_by_: The trachea (windpipe) is reinforced by C-shaped cartilage rings. Cilia move mucus upward to trap debris.
the_trachea_splits_into_left_and_right: The trachea splits into left and right main bronchi, each entering a lung. They branch into smaller bronchioles.
300_million_grape_like_sacs_where_gas_: 300 million grape-like sacs where gas exchange occurs. O2 diffuses into blood; CO2 diffuses out. Surface area equals a tennis court.
the_diaphragm_relaxes_and_rises_reduci: The diaphragm relaxes and rises, reducing lung volume. CO2-rich air is pushed out through the same pathway in reverse.
follow_a_meal_from_mouth_through_the_e: Follow a meal from mouth through the entire digestive system.
teeth_mechanically_break_food_down_sal: Teeth mechanically break food down. Salivary amylase begins starch digestion. The tongue shapes food into a bolus.
swallowing_pushes_the_bolus_past_the_e: Swallowing pushes the bolus past the epiglottis. Peristaltic waves move it down the 25cm esophagus in about 8 seconds.
gastric_acid_ph_1_5_3_5_and_pepsin_bre: Gastric acid (pH 1.5-3.5) and pepsin break down proteins. Churning produces chyme over 2-4 hours.
the_first_25cm_of_the_small_intestine_: The first 25cm of the small intestine receives bile from the liver/gallbladder and enzymes from the pancreas.
most_nutrient_absorption_occurs_here_v: Most nutrient absorption occurs here via villi and microvilli, increasing surface area 600-fold. 6-7 meters long.
water_and_electrolytes_are_reabsorbed_: Water and electrolytes are reabsorbed. Gut bacteria ferment remaining fiber, producing vitamins K and B12.
waste_is_compacted_and_stored_in_the_r: Waste is compacted and stored in the rectum until defecation. The entire journey takes 24-72 hours.
trace_a_reflex_arc_from_stimulus_to_re: Trace a reflex arc from stimulus to response.
a_sensory_receptor_in_the_skin_detects: A sensory receptor in the skin detects a painful stimulus (like touching a hot surface) and generates an electrical signal.
the_signal_travels_along_a_sensory_aff: The signal travels along a sensory (afferent) neuron toward the spinal cord at up to 120 m/s via saltatory conduction.
in_the_dorsal_horn_the_sensory_neuron_: In the dorsal horn, the sensory neuron synapses with an interneuron. For reflexes, the signal does not need to reach the brain.
the_interneuron_in_the_spinal_gray_mat: The interneuron in the spinal gray matter integrates the signal and relays it to a motor neuron.
the_motor_efferent_neuron_carries_the_: The motor (efferent) neuron carries the command signal from the ventral horn down to the target muscle.
acetylcholine_released_at_the_neuromus: Acetylcholine released at the neuromuscular junction causes muscle contraction. You pull your hand away before feeling pain.
meanwhile_a_copy_of_the_signal_ascends: Meanwhile, a copy of the signal ascends to the somatosensory cortex. You consciously feel pain about 0.5 seconds after the reflex.

route_blood_0_scope: The marker shows the whole heart; this step follows its right atrium.
route_blood_1_scope: The right ventricle is a chamber inside the heart shown by this marker.
route_blood_3_scope: The alveoli marker locates the exchange region. Blood stays in surrounding capillaries; it does not enter the air sacs.
route_blood_4_scope: The lungs marker locates the region. Pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs to the left atrium; individual veins are not drawn here.
route_blood_5_scope: The marker shows the whole heart; this step follows its left atrium.
route_blood_6_detail: The left ventricle fills through the mitral valve and generates pressure to send blood into the systemic circulation.
route_blood_6_scope: The left ventricle is a chamber inside the heart shown by this marker.
route_blood_8_scope: The femoral artery is one example of a delivery vessel. Exchange with body tissues happens downstream in capillaries, not in this artery.
route_air_1_detail: Air passes through the pharynx toward the larynx. The oropharynx and laryngopharynx also carry swallowed food; the nasopharynx carries air.
route_air_3_detail: Cartilage helps hold the trachea open. Mucus traps particles, and cilia move the mucus toward the throat.
route_air_5_detail: Many tiny alveoli provide a large, thin exchange surface. Oxygen diffuses into nearby capillary blood, while carbon dioxide diffuses toward alveolar air.
route_air_6_detail: During quiet breathing, the inspiratory muscles relax and elastic recoil reduces lung volume. Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, so air flows out. Forced exhalation also recruits muscles.
route_air_6_scope: The diaphragm marker shows a breathing muscle. Air travels through the airways, not through the diaphragm.
route_food_0_scope: The mandible is a jaw-bone landmark that supports chewing. Food stays in the mouth cavity; it does not travel through the bone.
route_food_1_detail: Swallowing moves the food bolus through the pharynx into the esophagus. Coordinated muscle contractions propel it toward the stomach while the airway is protected.
route_food_1_scope: The marker shows the pharynx. The esophagus continues below it and is not a separate marker in this catalog.
route_food_3_scope: The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine; the marker represents the larger organ.
route_food_4_detail: Folds, villi, and microvilli increase the small intestine’s absorptive surface. Most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine.
route_food_4_scope: The jejunum and ileum are regions of the small intestine; the marker represents the larger organ.
route_food_5_detail: The large intestine absorbs remaining water and electrolytes and helps form feces. Gut microbes ferment some material that escaped digestion.
route_food_6_detail: Feces are held in the rectum, the final storage region of the large intestine, before leaving through the anal canal and anus. The bladder stores urine and is not part of this food route.
route_food_6_scope: The marker shows the large intestine. The rectum is its terminal storage region; this marker is not a separate rectal outline.
route_nerve_0_detail: In this hand-withdrawal example, a potentially damaging stimulus on the palm side of the index finger activates sensory nerve endings in the skin.
route_nerve_0_scope: The skin marker represents a tissue type. The example stimulus is on the finger, not at the marker’s body location.
route_nerve_1_detail: Sensory axons from this part of the finger travel in the median nerve toward the cervical spinal cord, entering through dorsal roots. A peripheral nerve contains many axons, not just one neuron.
route_nerve_1_scope: The median nerve carries the sensory fibers used in this example. Its motor fibers have other roles.
route_nerve_2_detail: Sensory input reaches spinal circuits. A withdrawal response can begin without waiting for a conscious decision, while information also travels toward the brain.
route_nerve_2_scope: The marker shows the spinal cord as a whole. This upper-limb example uses cervical spinal circuits.
route_nerve_3_detail: Spinal interneurons link sensory input to motor output, helping activate withdrawal muscles and inhibit opposing muscles.
route_nerve_3_scope: Interneurons lie within spinal gray matter; the whole-cord marker does not show individual cells.
route_nerve_4_detail: Motor axons leave the spinal cord through ventral roots. Axons to the biceps travel through the brachial plexus and its musculocutaneous nerve branch.
route_nerve_4_scope: The marker shows the brachial plexus network. The musculocutaneous nerve branch to the biceps is not separately drawn.
route_nerve_5_detail: Acetylcholine signaling at neuromuscular junctions activates muscle fibers. Biceps contraction contributes to elbow flexion as the arm withdraws; other muscles also take part.
route_nerve_6_detail: Ascending pathways carry information toward the brain for conscious perception. Brain pathways can also modify spinal reflexes; awareness and withdrawal are not separated by one fixed delay.
route_nerve_6_scope: The marker shows the brain as a whole. Perception involves networks, not a single point at this marker.
route_intestine_fact: Small refers to its narrower diameter. Its folded lining, villi, and microvilli increase the area available for absorption; length and surface-area estimates depend on how they are measured.
route_gluteal_fact: Gluteus maximus weakness impairs forceful hip extension, such as rising from a chair. Trendelenburg gait is associated with hip-abductor dysfunction, especially gluteus medius and minimus. The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus.
route_check_blood_direction_prompt: Pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood. Why are they called arteries?
route_check_blood_direction_rich: Arteries must always carry oxygen-rich blood.
route_check_blood_direction_rich_feedbac: Oxygen content varies with the circuit. It does not define an artery.
route_check_blood_direction_away: They carry blood away from the heart.
route_check_blood_direction_away_feedbac: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it toward the heart.
route_check_blood_direction_lungs: Every vessel connected to a lung is an artery.
route_check_blood_direction_lungs_feedba: Pulmonary veins also connect to the lungs. Direction relative to the heart distinguishes arteries from veins.
route_check_blood_return_prompt: After gas exchange in the lungs, where does blood go next?
route_check_blood_return_right: To the right atrium through the venae cavae.
route_check_blood_return_right_feedback: The venae cavae return blood from the body. Blood from the lungs enters the left atrium.
route_check_blood_return_ventricle: To the right ventricle through pulmonary arteries.
route_check_blood_return_ventricle_feedb: That reverses pulmonary arterial flow. Pulmonary arteries carry blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs.
route_check_blood_return_left: To the left atrium through pulmonary veins.
route_check_blood_return_left_feedback: Pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
route_check_air_exchange_prompt: What crosses between alveolar air and nearby blood during gas exchange?
route_check_air_exchange_gases: Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across a thin barrier.
route_check_air_exchange_gases_feedback: The gases diffuse across the air–blood barrier. Blood remains in capillaries.
route_check_air_exchange_bubbles: Whole air bubbles enter the blood.
route_check_air_exchange_bubbles_feedbac: Normal gas exchange transfers gas molecules, not air bubbles, into blood.
route_check_air_exchange_diaphragm: Air passes through the diaphragm into the blood.
route_check_air_exchange_diaphragm_feedb: The diaphragm helps change chest volume. Gas exchange occurs at the alveoli and surrounding capillaries.
route_check_air_recoil_prompt: During quiet breathing at rest, what helps air flow out?
route_check_air_recoil_contract_feedback: This enlarges the chest during inhalation. Quiet exhalation follows relaxation of inspiratory muscles.
route_check_air_recoil_relax: Inspiratory muscles relax and the lungs recoil.
route_check_air_recoil_relax_feedback: Elastic recoil reduces lung volume, raising alveolar pressure above atmospheric pressure so air flows out.
route_check_air_recoil_gravity: Gravity pulls all air downward out of the lungs.
route_check_air_recoil_gravity_feedback: Airflow follows a pressure difference. It is not defined by an upward or downward direction.
route_check_food_exit_prompt: Which route carries feces out of the digestive tract?
route_check_food_exit_rectum_feedback: Feces pass through the rectum and anal canal to the anus. Urine leaves by a separate route.
route_check_food_exit_bladder_feedback: The bladder stores urine. The bladder and urethra are urinary structures, not the route for feces.
route_check_food_exit_gallbladder_feedba: The gallbladder stores bile used in digestion. It does not store or expel feces.
route_check_food_surface_prompt: How do intestinal villi support nutrient absorption?
route_check_food_surface_chunks: They let large food chunks pass directly into blood.
route_check_food_surface_chunks_feedback: Nutrients must cross the intestinal lining. Whole food chunks do not normally enter blood.
route_check_food_surface_block: They block all movement through the intestine.
route_check_food_surface_block_feedback: Villi line the intestinal wall; they do not seal the passage through the intestine.
route_check_food_surface_area: They increase the surface available for absorption.
route_check_food_surface_area_feedback: Villi and microvilli provide more absorptive surface within the intestinal lining.
route_check_nerve_hand_prompt: In this example, which nerve carries sensory input from the palm side of the index finger?
route_check_nerve_hand_sciatic_feedback: The sciatic nerve serves the lower limb. It does not carry sensation from this finger.
route_check_nerve_hand_median_feedback: The median nerve carries sensory fibers from this part of the index finger toward the spinal cord.
route_check_nerve_hand_femoral_feedback: The femoral nerve serves parts of the lower limb, not the hand.
route_check_nerve_spinal_prompt: How can withdrawal begin without waiting for a conscious decision?
route_check_nerve_spinal_circuit: Spinal circuits link sensory input to motor output.
route_check_nerve_spinal_circuit_feedbac: Spinal circuits can initiate the reflex while information also travels toward the brain.
route_check_nerve_spinal_muscle: The muscle makes a decision without nerve signals.
route_check_nerve_spinal_muscle_feedback: Muscle fibers respond to motor signals. They do not replace the sensory and spinal parts of this reflex.
route_check_nerve_spinal_never: No information about the stimulus ever reaches the brain.
route_check_nerve_spinal_never_feedback: Information also travels upward for perception, and brain pathways can modify spinal reflexes.

route_air_2_detail: Air passes between the vocal folds in the larynx. Coordinated laryngeal closure, including movement of the epiglottis, helps protect the airway during swallowing.
route_food_2_detail: Gastric acid helps unfold proteins and activate pepsin, the enzyme that begins their digestion. Muscular mixing combines food and gastric juices into chyme, which is gradually released into the duodenum.
route_food_3_detail: The duodenum receives bile made by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, along with pancreatic enzymes and bicarbonate. These secretions support digestion and help neutralize acidic chyme.
route_blood_5_detail: Blood from the pulmonary veins enters the left atrium and flows through the mitral valve into the relaxed left ventricle. Atrial contraction adds to ventricular filling.
tour_ref_skeletal_0_narration: The skull protects the brain and supports the face. Most of its 22 bones meet at strong seams called sutures; the lower jaw moves at a joint.
tour_ref_skeletal_0_recall: Which bony structure surrounds the brain and includes the movable lower jaw?
tour_ref_skeletal_1_narration: The vertebral column supports the trunk and protects the spinal cord. Adult anatomy usually includes 24 separate vertebrae, plus the sacrum and coccyx formed from fused segments.
tour_ref_skeletal_1_recall: Which column of bones surrounds the spinal cord and supports the trunk?
tour_ref_skeletal_2_narration: The ribs form a protective cage around the heart and lungs. Their joints and costal cartilages allow movement as the chest changes volume during breathing.
tour_ref_skeletal_2_recall: Which curved bones form the protective cage around the heart and lungs?
tour_ref_skeletal_3_narration: The femur is the thigh bone, extending from the hip to the knee. It transmits loads and provides attachment sites for muscles that move the hip and knee.
tour_ref_skeletal_3_recall: Which long bone connects the hip to the knee?
tour_ref_skeletal_4_narration: The bony pelvis transfers loads from the spine to the lower limbs. It also surrounds and protects organs in the pelvic cavity.
tour_ref_skeletal_4_recall: Which bony ring transfers loads from the spine to the lower limbs?
tour_ref_muscular_0_narration: The diaphragm separates the chest and abdomen. Its contraction increases chest volume during inhalation; relaxation and elastic recoil contribute to quiet exhalation.
tour_ref_muscular_0_recall: Which dome-shaped muscle separates the chest and abdomen and helps draw air in?
tour_ref_muscular_1_narration: The deltoid covers the shoulder. Its middle fibers help raise the arm to the side, while its front and back fibers contribute to different shoulder movements.
tour_ref_muscular_1_recall: Which muscle covers the shoulder and helps raise the arm to the side?
tour_ref_muscular_2_narration: The rectus abdominis runs along the front of the abdomen. It flexes the trunk and works with other abdominal muscles to support the trunk and compress abdominal contents.
tour_ref_muscular_2_recall: Which paired muscle on the front of the abdomen helps bend the trunk forward?
tour_ref_muscular_3_narration: The quadriceps group on the front of the thigh extends the knee. One member, rectus femoris, also crosses the hip and contributes to hip flexion.
tour_ref_muscular_3_recall: Which muscle group on the front of the thigh straightens the knee?
tour_ref_muscular_4_narration: The gastrocnemius crosses the knee and ankle. It helps point the foot downward and flex the knee; its force reaches the heel through the Achilles tendon.
tour_ref_muscular_4_recall: Which superficial calf muscle crosses both the knee and ankle and joins the Achilles tendon?
tour_ref_circulatory_0_narration: The heart has four chambers. Its right side pumps blood through the lungs, and its left side pumps blood through the systemic circulation.
tour_ref_circulatory_0_recall: Which four-chambered organ pumps blood through the pulmonary and systemic circuits?
tour_ref_circulatory_1_narration: The aorta carries blood from the left ventricle into the systemic circulation. Its branches supply the heart itself, head, limbs, and trunk.
tour_ref_circulatory_1_recall: Which major artery receives blood directly from the left ventricle?
tour_ref_circulatory_2_narration: The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle. A severe, sustained reduction in this supply can damage the muscle; the blood inside the chambers does not replace its arterial supply.
tour_ref_circulatory_2_recall: Which arteries supply the heart muscle itself?
tour_ref_circulatory_3_narration: The common carotid arteries travel through the neck and divide into internal and external branches. Internal branches help supply the brain; external branches supply much of the face and scalp.
tour_ref_circulatory_3_recall: Which paired arteries in the neck divide into internal and external branches?
tour_ref_nervous_0_narration: The brain includes the cerebrum, cerebellum, and brainstem. Interconnected networks support perception, thought, movement, and regulation of body functions.
tour_ref_nervous_0_recall: Which whole organ contains the cerebrum, cerebellum, and brainstem?
tour_ref_nervous_1_narration: The cerebral cortex is the outer gray matter of the cerebrum. Its connected regions contribute to sensation, voluntary movement, language, and thought.
tour_ref_nervous_1_recall: Which outer layer of the cerebrum contains gray matter involved in sensation and voluntary movement?
tour_ref_nervous_2_narration: The spinal cord carries signals between the brain and body. Local spinal circuits can also coordinate reflexes without waiting for a conscious decision.
tour_ref_nervous_2_recall: Which nervous-system structure runs inside the vertebral column and contains local reflex circuits?
tour_ref_nervous_3_narration: The vagus nerve connects the brainstem with many organs in the chest and abdomen. It carries sensory information inward and parasympathetic signals that influence functions such as heart rate and digestion.
tour_ref_nervous_3_recall: Which cranial nerve travels from the brainstem to many chest and abdominal organs?
tour_ref_lymphatic_0_narration: The thymus supports T-cell maturation and selection, including mechanisms that limit reactions against the body's own tissues. It becomes smaller and contains more fatty tissue with age.
tour_ref_lymphatic_0_recall: Which lymphoid organ is a major site of T-cell maturation?
tour_ref_lymphatic_1_narration: The spleen filters blood, removes aging or damaged red blood cells, and supports immune responses to material carried in the blood. Lymph nodes filter lymph instead.
tour_ref_lymphatic_1_recall: Which organ filters blood and removes aging red blood cells?
tour_ref_lymphatic_2_narration: Cervical lymph nodes filter lymph draining from regions of the head and neck. They can enlarge during an immune response, but enlargement has more than one possible cause.
tour_ref_lymphatic_2_recall: Which small structures in the neck filter lymph draining from nearby tissues?
tour_ref_lymphatic_3_narration: Red bone marrow contains blood-forming stem cells. They give rise to blood-cell lineages; platelets are fragments released from large cells called megakaryocytes.
tour_ref_lymphatic_3_recall: Which tissue inside certain bones contains stem cells that produce blood-cell lineages?
tour_ref_organs_0_narration: The lungs contain branching airways and many alveoli. Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across the thin barrier between alveolar air and surrounding capillary blood.
tour_ref_organs_0_recall: Which paired chest organs contain the airways and alveoli used for gas exchange?
tour_ref_organs_1_narration: The liver makes bile, processes nutrients, stores glycogen, and makes many blood proteins. Bile helps disperse dietary fat into small droplets; digestive enzymes break fat molecules down.
tour_ref_organs_1_recall: Which organ makes bile and stores glucose in the form of glycogen?
tour_ref_organs_2_narration: The stomach mixes food with gastric juice to form chyme. Acid helps unfold proteins and activate pepsin, while controlled emptying delivers chyme to the small intestine.
tour_ref_organs_2_recall: Which muscular organ mixes food with gastric juice before releasing chyme to the small intestine?
tour_ref_organs_3_narration: The kidneys contain nephrons that filter fluid from blood and modify it by reabsorption and secretion. Blood cells normally remain in vessels; most filtered water and useful substances return to the blood.
tour_ref_organs_3_recall: Which paired organs use nephrons to form filtrate and modify it into urine?
tour_ref_integumentary_0_narration: The epidermis is the outer skin layer and has no blood vessels. Its barrier reduces water loss and entry of harmful substances; renewal varies with body site, age, and other conditions.
tour_ref_integumentary_0_recall: Which outer skin layer forms a barrier and contains no blood vessels?
tour_ref_integumentary_1_narration: The dermis lies beneath the epidermis. Its connective tissue provides strength and elasticity, and it contains blood vessels, nerves, and many skin appendages.
tour_ref_integumentary_1_recall: Which connective-tissue skin layer lies beneath the epidermis and contains blood vessels?
tour_ref_integumentary_2_narration: A hair follicle surrounds the growing hair root. A small smooth muscle attached to it can pull the hair upright, contributing to goosebumps.
tour_ref_integumentary_2_recall: Which structure surrounds a growing hair root and connects to a small goosebump-producing muscle?
tour_ref_integumentary_3_narration: Melanocytes make melanin and transfer it to nearby skin cells. Melanin contributes to skin color and absorbs some ultraviolet radiation, but does not prevent all UV damage.
tour_ref_integumentary_3_recall: Which pigment-producing cells make melanin and pass it to neighboring skin cells?
tour_ref_respiratory_0_narration: The nasal cavity helps warm, humidify, and filter incoming air. Its conchae increase the air's contact with the moist lining.
tour_ref_respiratory_0_recall: Which space inside the nose warms and humidifies incoming air?
tour_ref_respiratory_1_narration: The larynx connects the pharynx and trachea. Air moving between appropriately positioned vocal folds can make them vibrate to produce voice; coordinated closure helps protect the airway during swallowing.
tour_ref_respiratory_1_recall: Which voice-producing structure lies between the pharynx and trachea?
tour_ref_respiratory_2_narration: The main bronchi carry air from the trachea into the lungs. Their branches lead to smaller airways and eventually to regions where gas exchange occurs.
tour_ref_respiratory_2_recall: Which two main airway branches carry air from the trachea into the lungs?
tour_ref_respiratory_3_narration: Alveoli are small air spaces closely associated with capillaries. A thin exchange barrier and large combined surface support diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
tour_ref_respiratory_3_recall: Which tiny air spaces provide a thin surface for exchange with nearby capillary blood?
tour_ref_endocrine_0_narration: The pituitary lies below the hypothalamus. Its anterior lobe makes several hormones; its posterior lobe releases hormones made in the hypothalamus. It influences many endocrine functions, but does not control every gland.
tour_ref_endocrine_0_recall: Which gland below the hypothalamus has anterior and posterior lobes with different hormone roles?
tour_ref_endocrine_1_narration: The thyroid lies at the front of the neck near the trachea. Thyroid hormones influence energy use, growth, and development rather than acting as an on-off switch for metabolism.
tour_ref_endocrine_1_recall: Which butterfly-shaped neck gland produces hormones that influence metabolic rate?
tour_ref_endocrine_2_narration: The adrenal cortex makes steroid hormones, including cortisol and aldosterone. The inner medulla makes catecholamines such as adrenaline. This marker represents the whole adrenal gland.
tour_ref_endocrine_2_recall: Which glands above the kidneys have a steroid-producing cortex and an adrenaline-producing medulla?
tour_ref_endocrine_3_narration: Pancreatic islets contain several hormone-producing cell types. Beta cells release insulin and alpha cells release glucagon; these hormones help regulate blood glucose through different effects on target tissues.
tour_ref_endocrine_3_recall: Which endocrine cell clusters in the pancreas contain insulin-producing beta cells?
tour_ref_reproductive_0_narration: The testes contain seminiferous tubules where sperm develop. Other cells make testosterone. Their scrotal location helps maintain a temperature suitable for sperm production.
tour_ref_reproductive_0_recall: Which organs contain sperm-producing seminiferous tubules and cells that make testosterone?
tour_ref_reproductive_1_narration: The uterus has a muscular wall and an inner lining called the endometrium. Implantation normally occurs in this lining; during a menstrual cycle without pregnancy, much of its functional layer is shed.
tour_ref_reproductive_1_recall: Which muscular organ contains the endometrium where implantation normally occurs?
tour_ref_reproductive_2_narration: The ovaries contain follicles with immature oocytes and produce hormones such as estrogen and progesterone. Ovulation usually releases one oocyte in an ovulatory cycle, but cycle patterns vary.
tour_ref_reproductive_2_recall: Which paired organs contain oocyte-bearing follicles and produce estrogen and progesterone?
tour_ref_reproductive_3_narration: The placenta supports exchange between maternal and fetal circulations. Their blood normally remains in separate spaces while gases, nutrients, and wastes cross a tissue barrier; the placenta is not an absolute barrier to all substances.
tour_ref_reproductive_3_recall: Which temporary organ supports exchange between maternal and fetal circulations during pregnancy?

link_ref_conn_1_desc: Pulmonary blood flow brings blood close to alveolar air. Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across a thin tissue barrier down their own partial-pressure gradients; blood and air normally remain separate.
link_ref_conn_1_example: During exercise, ventilation and pulmonary blood flow can both increase to support gas exchange.
link_ref_conn_1_question: If the air–blood barrier becomes thicker, what happens to diffusion when other conditions stay the same?
link_ref_conn_1_explanation: A thicker barrier increases diffusion distance. Ventilation moves air and circulation moves blood; gas exchange between them depends on diffusion.
link_ref_conn_2_desc: At a skeletal neuromuscular junction, a motor neuron releases acetylcholine. This activates the muscle fiber and leads to calcium release inside it. Cardiac and smooth muscle have different control mechanisms.
link_ref_conn_2_example: To extend the knee, motor neurons activate quadriceps fibers. Tendons transmit their force to the skeleton.
link_ref_conn_2_question: If acetylcholine receptors at a skeletal neuromuscular junction are blocked, what is the immediate effect?
link_ref_conn_2_choice_0: The nerve signal activates the muscle fiber less effectively.
link_ref_conn_2_choice_1: The tendon produces a stronger nerve signal.
link_ref_conn_2_choice_2: The bone contracts instead of the muscle.
link_ref_conn_2_explanation: Acetylcholine must act on muscle-fiber receptors to initiate normal neuromuscular transmission. This example concerns skeletal muscle, not every type of muscle.
link_ref_conn_3_desc: Skeletal muscles transmit pulling forces through tendons. When that force acts across a joint, it can rotate bones; the effect depends on the joint position and the muscle's moment arm.
link_ref_conn_3_example: Biceps force reaches the radius through its tendon and contributes to elbow flexion. Other muscles also help flex the elbow.
link_ref_conn_3_question: Why can the biceps help rotate the forearm at the elbow?
link_ref_conn_3_choice_0: Its tendon transmits force at a distance from the joint's axis.
link_ref_conn_3_choice_1: Its fibers push the radius away from the humerus.
link_ref_conn_3_choice_2: The radius shortens when the muscle contracts.
link_ref_conn_3_explanation: A pulling force with a moment arm produces torque about the joint. Bone length does not shorten during this movement.
link_ref_conn_4_desc: Hypothalamic GnRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH. These hormones act on the gonads; gonadal hormones feed back to the brain and pituitary. Feedback patterns vary with the reproductive context.
link_ref_conn_4_example: In an ovulatory cycle, sustained high estradiol can produce positive feedback that helps trigger an LH surge.
link_ref_conn_4_question: Which organ releases FSH and LH into the blood?
link_ref_conn_4_choice_1: The hypothalamus, as another name for GnRH.
link_ref_conn_4_explanation: GnRH comes from the hypothalamus. FSH and LH come from the anterior pituitary and act on gonadal tissues.
link_ref_conn_5_desc: Lymphatic vessels collect excess tissue fluid and return it to venous blood. Lymph nodes bring lymph into contact with immune cells. Blood circulation and lymph flow support fluid balance and immune surveillance.
link_ref_conn_5_example: During an immune response, a draining lymph node may enlarge. A small cut does not always cause noticeable node swelling.
link_ref_conn_5_question: If lymph drainage from a tissue is obstructed, what is more likely?
link_ref_conn_5_choice_1: The tissue stops receiving all arterial blood immediately.
link_ref_conn_5_explanation: Blocked lymph drainage reduces the return of interstitial fluid to blood and can contribute to swelling. Lymph vessels and arteries have different roles.
link_ref_conn_6_desc: The hypothalamus links neural information with endocrine regulation. It controls many pituitary functions; some endocrine tissues also respond directly to blood chemistry or other signals.
link_ref_conn_6_example: In the stress axis, hypothalamic CRH promotes pituitary ACTH release. ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce cortisol, which contributes to negative feedback.
link_ref_conn_6_question: In this stress-axis example, what does rising cortisol usually do to upstream CRH and ACTH release?
link_ref_conn_6_choice_0: It helps reduce their release through negative feedback.
link_ref_conn_6_choice_1: It always increases both without limit.
link_ref_conn_6_choice_2: It turns the adrenal cortex into nervous tissue.
link_ref_conn_6_explanation: Cortisol feeds back to the hypothalamus and pituitary. Feedback regulates the pathway; it is not a claim that the pituitary controls every endocrine process.
link_ref_conn_7_desc: During quiet inhalation, the diaphragm and external intercostals expand the chest. Quiet exhalation mainly uses relaxation and elastic recoil. Airway walls contain smooth muscle that adjusts airway diameter.
link_ref_conn_7_example: As inspiratory muscles expand the chest, alveolar pressure briefly falls below atmospheric pressure and air flows inward.
link_ref_conn_7_question: What normally drives air out during quiet exhalation?
link_ref_conn_7_choice_0: Elastic recoil after inspiratory muscles relax raises alveolar pressure.
link_ref_conn_7_choice_1: The diaphragm actively pushes air through the lungs on every quiet breath.
link_ref_conn_7_choice_2: Airway smooth muscle pumps each breath like a heart.
link_ref_conn_7_explanation: Air flows from higher to lower pressure. Quiet expiration is mainly passive; forced expiration recruits additional muscles. Airway smooth muscle regulates resistance.
link_ref_conn_8_desc: Skin receptors convert mechanical, thermal, and potentially damaging stimuli into neural signals. Different receptor types and their connections contribute to touch, temperature, and pain perception.
link_ref_conn_8_example: Fingertip receptors provide detailed touch information. Perceiving shape or texture also requires processing in the nervous system.
link_ref_conn_8_question: Why is a touch receptor alone insufficient to identify an object's shape?
link_ref_conn_8_choice_0: Its signals must be processed with other sensory information by neural circuits.
link_ref_conn_8_choice_1: Shape is carried through the blood instead of nerves.
link_ref_conn_8_choice_2: Every skin receptor detects exactly the same stimulus.
link_ref_conn_8_explanation: Receptors begin sensory transduction. Perception depends on neural processing and information from populations of receptors, not one isolated ending.
link_ref_conn_9_desc: Much venous blood from digestive organs reaches the liver through the hepatic portal system before returning to the heart. The liver processes absorbed nutrients. Many long-chain dietary fats initially enter lymph instead.
link_ref_conn_9_example: After a meal, absorbed glucose reaches the liver in portal blood. The liver can store glucose as glycogen, while other tissues and hormones also help regulate blood glucose.
link_ref_conn_9_question: Which absorbed material commonly enters intestinal lymph before reaching blood?
link_ref_conn_9_explanation: Enterocytes package many long-chain lipids into chylomicrons that enter lacteals. Monosaccharides and amino acids mainly enter intestinal capillary blood.
link_ref_conn_10_desc: In adults, red bone marrow is a major site of blood-cell production. Blood-forming stem cells give rise to several cell lineages; platelets are fragments released by megakaryocytes. Some immune cells mature elsewhere.
link_ref_conn_10_example: Marrow in bones such as the pelvis and sternum supports blood-cell production. Developing T cells complete important maturation steps in the thymus.
link_ref_conn_10_choice_0: They are cell fragments released from megakaryocytes.
link_ref_conn_10_choice_1: They are fully formed red blood cells.
link_ref_conn_10_choice_2: They are hormones secreted by the thymus.
link_ref_conn_10_explanation: Megakaryocytes shed platelets that participate in hemostasis. A shared marrow origin does not make all formed elements the same cell type.
link_ref_mn_carpals_meaning: In each row, read from the thumb side toward the little-finger side. Proximal: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform. Distal: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate. The pisiform lies on the palm side of the triquetrum.
link_ref_mn_cranial_meaning: Occipital, parietal, frontal, temporal, ethmoid, sphenoid: six bone types, eight cranial bones. Parietal and temporal bones are paired; this is not a spatial sequence.
link_ref_mn_vertebrae_meaning: Seven cervical, twelve thoracic, and five lumbar vertebrae. These are the usual 24 separate adult vertebrae; the fused sacrum and coccyx are additional regions.
link_ref_mn_rotator_meaning: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis form the rotator cuff. They help stabilize the humeral head and have different movement actions.
link_ref_mn_erector_meaning: From lateral to medial: iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis. These are erector spinae columns, not the trapezius. They are not individually represented by this catalog's markers.
link_ref_mn_quad_meaning: Rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus intermedius, vastus medialis. All extend the knee; rectus femoris also crosses the hip. The letters group the four names rather than describing a spatial order.
link_ref_mn_heartvalves_meaning: Tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, aortic: valve order along the blood-flow route. Chambers, lung vessels, and the lungs lie between parts of this sequence; the valves are not adjacent stops.
link_ref_mn_aorta_meaning: Usual aortic arch branches: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, left subclavian artery. Branching variants occur.
link_ref_mn_cranialn_meaning: Cranial nerves I–XII: olfactory, optic, oculomotor, trochlear, trigeminal, abducens, facial, vestibulocochlear, glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory, hypoglossal. This cue names the nerves; it does not describe all their functions.
link_ref_mn_brachial_meaning: Roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches: the major organizational levels of the brachial plexus. Its roots are anterior rami, usually C5–T1, rather than the dorsal and ventral roots of the spinal cord.
link_ref_mn_immune_meaning: Neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils: a common adult peripheral-blood abundance pattern. Proportions vary with age and health; this is not a universal ranking or a list of every immune cell.
link_ref_mn_liver_meaning: Couinaud's scheme divides the liver into eight functional segments with portal inflow territories. Major hepatic veins run between many territories. This is a functional segmentation scheme, not the visible surface lobes.
link_ref_mn_intestine_meaning: From the lumen outward: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, then serosa or adventitia. The outer covering depends on the organ region; the stomach also has an oblique muscle layer.
link_ref_mn_skin_meaning: In thick skin, from superficial to deep: stratum corneum, lucidum, granulosum, spinosum, basale. Stratum lucidum is characteristic of thick skin on palms and soles; thin skin lacks a distinct lucidum layer.
link_ref_mn_resp_meaning: Nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli: a simplified inward air route. The second B includes smaller bronchioles; alveolar ducts and sacs connect to the alveoli.
link_ref_mn_pituitary_meaning: Anterior pituitary: FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH, prolactin, growth hormone. This cue lists six major hormones; it excludes posterior-pituitary release of oxytocin and vasopressin.
link_ref_mn_repro_meaning: Prophase I, metaphase I, anaphase I, telophase I. Crossing over occurs during prophase I; homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I. Sister chromatids normally separate during meiosis II.

case_ref_case_1_presentation: A 16-year-old runner reports aching around the front of the knee after increasing training. Stairs and squats make it worse. There was no single injury, and no locking is reported.
case_ref_case_1_question: Which joint region would you examine first, and which clues support that choice?
case_ref_case_1_answer: The patellofemoral region, where the kneecap meets the femur.
case_ref_case_1_explanation: Anterior knee pain with stairs or squatting is consistent with patellofemoral pain. The patella transmits quadriceps force and contacts the femur as the knee bends. Several surrounding tissues can contribute to pain; articular cartilage itself has no pain-sensing nerves.
case_ref_case_1_hint: Use the location of the pain and activities that load a bent knee. A symptom pattern can suggest a region without identifying one damaged tissue.
case_ref_case_1_limit: This history does not prove abnormal patellar tracking or cartilage injury. Examination is needed to distinguish other causes of anterior knee pain.
case_ref_case_1_scope: The marker shows the patella, not a diagnosed lesion or the whole joint surface.
case_ref_case_2_presentation: An adult who often works overhead has gradually developed shoulder pain. Raising the arm is painful, and lying on that shoulder can disturb sleep. No examination or imaging results are given.
case_ref_case_2_question: Which muscle–tendon group is relevant, and can these clues establish a tear?
case_ref_case_2_answer: The rotator cuff is relevant; pain alone does not establish a tendon tear.
case_ref_case_2_explanation: The rotator cuff helps center the humeral head in the glenoid during movement. Supraspinatus is one of its four muscles, and its tendon passes beneath the acromion. Rotator-cuff disorders can cause pain with overhead activity, but several shoulder conditions have similar symptoms.
case_ref_case_2_hint: Think about the muscles that stabilize the humeral head while the arm moves. Distinguish pain-limited movement from demonstrated weakness.
case_ref_case_2_limit: The vignette cannot distinguish tendinopathy, bursitis, a tear, or other causes. Physical examination and, when appropriate, imaging provide additional evidence.
case_ref_case_2_scope: The marker represents the rotator cuff group; it does not isolate the supraspinatus tendon or show a tear.
case_ref_case_3_presentation: During a supervised exercise demonstration, an adolescent's pulse speeds up during running and gradually slows during recovery. The lesson is about the normal control of heart rate.
case_ref_case_3_question: Which structure normally initiates the heartbeat, and how can its rate change during exercise?
case_ref_case_3_answer: The sinoatrial (SA) node, modified by autonomic signals and circulating hormones.
case_ref_case_3_explanation: Pacemaker cells in the SA node, located in the right atrium, normally initiate electrical activity. Sympathetic activity and catecholamines increase their firing rate, while parasympathetic activity slows it. Exercise changes the balance of these influences.
case_ref_case_3_hint: Separate the heart's own pacemaker activity from the signals that adjust its rate.
case_ref_case_3_limit: A pulse observation does not identify every rhythm. This normal-physiology example does not establish that an unexplained racing or irregular heartbeat is benign.
case_ref_case_3_scope: The marker shows the whole heart. The SA node is a small region of the right atrium and is not separately outlined.
case_ref_case_4_presentation: An adult has intermittent tingling on the palm side of the thumb, index finger, and middle finger, especially at night. The little finger is unaffected. The cause has not yet been established.
case_ref_case_4_question: Which nerve's sensory territory fits these clues, and where could it be compressed?
case_ref_case_4_answer: The median nerve; compression at the carpal tunnel is one possible explanation.
case_ref_case_4_explanation: In the hand, the median nerve supplies the palmar thumb, index, middle, and thumb-side half of the ring finger. It passes beneath the flexor retinaculum at the wrist. Compression there can cause carpal tunnel symptoms; the little finger is mainly in the ulnar nerve territory.
case_ref_case_4_hint: Map the affected digits and compare them with the unaffected little finger. A nerve territory helps localize a problem.
case_ref_case_4_limit: The pattern supports a median-nerve hypothesis but does not prove the site or cause. The vignette does not establish that typing caused the symptoms.
case_ref_case_4_scope: The marker locates the median nerve schematically; it does not display an individual person's compression site.
case_ref_case_5_presentation: An adolescent has a persistently enlarged, painless neck lymph node, drenching night sweats, and unexplained weight loss. This fictional case calls for prompt clinical assessment.
case_ref_case_5_question: Why do these clues require further investigation, and why can they not establish Hodgkin lymphoma by themselves?
case_ref_case_5_answer: Persistent enlargement with systemic symptoms warrants investigation; tissue and clinical evidence are needed to determine the cause.
case_ref_case_5_explanation: Lymph nodes filter lymph and support immune responses. Infection, inflammatory disease, and malignancy can all cause enlargement. Hodgkin lymphoma is one possible cause of this pattern, and diagnosis typically involves lymph-node tissue examined by specialists.
case_ref_case_5_hint: A lymph node can enlarge for several reasons. Distinguish a reason to investigate from proof of a particular disease.
case_ref_case_5_limit: Node size, texture, and symptoms alone cannot identify the lymphoma type or exclude other causes. This is an exercise in recognizing uncertainty, not making a diagnosis from a short story.
case_ref_case_5_scope: The cervical-node marker shows a lymph-node region, not a biopsy result or a specific enlarged node.
case_ref_case_6_presentation: In a fictional emergency case, a person with type 1 diabetes has missed insulin, becomes confused, and breathes deeply and rapidly. Hospital tests show high glucose, elevated ketones, and metabolic acidosis.
case_ref_case_6_question: How can inadequate insulin lead to acidosis, and why does breathing change?
case_ref_case_6_answer: Insulin deficiency promotes ketone production; increased ventilation helps lower carbon dioxide during metabolic acidosis.
case_ref_case_6_explanation: Pancreatic beta cells normally produce insulin. In type 1 diabetes, loss of beta-cell function creates a need for replacement insulin. Inadequate insulin can promote fat breakdown and hepatic ketone production. Accumulating ketoacids lower blood pH; deeper ventilation reduces carbon dioxide as partial compensation.
case_ref_case_6_hint: Link the missing hormone to fat metabolism, then connect an acid–base disturbance to ventilation.
case_ref_case_6_limit: High glucose alone does not establish diabetic ketoacidosis; ketosis and acidosis are also essential findings. DKA is a medical emergency, and compensatory breathing does not correct the underlying insulin deficiency.
case_ref_case_6_scope: The islet marker represents endocrine cell clusters in the pancreas; beta cells are one cell type within them.
case_ref_case_7_presentation: A child falls onto the shoulder while cycling. Imaging confirms a fracture through the middle region of the clavicle. The task is to explain the bone's mechanical role.
case_ref_case_7_question: How does the clavicle's role help explain a fracture after force reaches the shoulder?
case_ref_case_7_answer: The clavicle acts as a strut and transmits force between the shoulder girdle and the trunk.
case_ref_case_7_explanation: The clavicle links the scapula to the sternum and helps hold the shoulder away from the chest. Loads at the shoulder can stress its curved shaft. Midshaft fractures are common, but their mechanics cannot be reduced to a claim that the bone has no muscular attachments.
case_ref_case_7_hint: Trace a load from the shoulder toward the sternum. Consider the bone's shape as well as its connections.
case_ref_case_7_limit: This case provides imaging confirmation. Pain or deformity alone does not describe the fracture pattern, and treatment depends on factors beyond this anatomy example.
case_ref_case_7_scope: The marker shows the clavicle as a whole, not the fracture line seen on imaging.
case_ref_case_8_presentation: During an uphill walk at high altitude, a hiker breathes faster than during a similar walk near sea level. The example concerns the effect of altitude on inspired oxygen.
case_ref_case_8_question: Does altitude mainly change oxygen's percentage in air or its inspired partial pressure? Explain the difference.
case_ref_case_8_answer: The oxygen fraction remains about 21%, while lower atmospheric pressure reduces inspired oxygen partial pressure.
case_ref_case_8_explanation: At altitude, lower barometric pressure lowers inspired and alveolar oxygen partial pressure. This can reduce oxygen loading into blood. Increased ventilation is one compensatory response; acclimatization includes additional changes over time.
case_ref_case_8_hint: Partial pressure depends on both a gas's fraction and the total pressure. A similar fraction does not guarantee a similar partial pressure.
case_ref_case_8_limit: This example does not identify one 'most stressed' structure or determine whether a person has altitude illness. Symptoms need context beyond the oxygen-pressure relationship.
case_ref_case_8_scope: The alveoli marker locates the gas-exchange region; it does not display oxygen pressure or measure a person's oxygenation.

fact_ref_skeletal_desc: Bones support movement, protect organs, store minerals, and house blood-forming marrow. Counts depend on age and anatomical conventions.
fact_ref_femur_fn: The femur is the thigh bone and usually the longest bone. Its head meets the hip socket, and its lower end forms part of the knee. Shape, bone tissue, and loading direction all influence its strength.
fact_ref_femur_clinicalKid: Your femur is your thigh bone. It joins your hip to your knee and supports you when you stand and move. Bones are living tissues that grow and change.
fact_ref_muscular_desc: Muscles produce force, support posture and movement, and generate heat. Skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle have different roles.
fact_ref_circulatory_desc: The heart and blood vessels circulate blood, transporting gases, nutrients, hormones, and wastes. Flow changes with the body’s needs.
fact_ref_heart_fn: A muscular pump with four chambers. The right side sends blood toward the lungs; the left side sends it around the body. Cardiac output depends on heart rate and the blood volume pumped per beat.
fact_ref_lymphatic_desc: Lymphatic vessels return tissue fluid and absorb dietary fats. Lymph nodes, thymus, and spleen support immune function.
fact_ref_integumentary_desc: Skin, hair, nails, and glands support the body’s barrier, temperature regulation, and sensation. Skin size and renewal vary.
fact_ref_respiratory_desc: Airways conduct air; alveoli exchange gases with blood. Breathing rate, breath volume, and gas exchange are related but different.
fact_ref_pituitary_fn: The pituitary lies in the sella turcica. Its anterior lobe produces hormones including GH, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH, and prolactin. Its posterior lobe stores and releases ADH and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus. It regulates many endocrine pathways, but not all.
fact_ref_pituitary_clinicalKid: Your pituitary is a small gland below your brain. It releases hormones that help control growth and other body functions. It works with the hypothalamus, and other glands can also respond to signals in the blood.
fact_ref_skeletal_0_question: Why can the number of separate bones change as a child grows?
fact_ref_skeletal_0_text: Some developing bones fuse as the skeleton matures. The familiar adult count of 206 is a conventional reference, not a count to apply unchanged to every age.
fact_ref_skeletal_1_question: Is a bone living tissue or just a hard support?
fact_ref_skeletal_1_text: Bone contains living cells and a blood supply. Cells build, maintain, and remove bone tissue, allowing the skeleton to grow, repair, and remodel.
fact_ref_skeletal_2_question: Why does bone need both minerals and collagen?
fact_ref_skeletal_2_text: Minerals give bone hardness, while collagen helps it resist pulling without being excessively brittle. Bone's shape and internal organization also influence how it bears a load.
fact_ref_muscular_0_question: Why does walking need muscles that stabilize as well as muscles that move?
fact_ref_muscular_0_text: Movement depends on coordinated muscle activity. Some muscles produce a movement, others oppose or control it, and others stabilize a joint or body segment. Which muscles contribute depends on the movement and how it is performed.
fact_ref_muscular_1_question: Does heart muscle stay contracted between beats?
fact_ref_muscular_1_text: Each heartbeat includes contraction and relaxation, which allow pumping and filling. At a constant 70 beats per minute, the arithmetic gives 100,800 beats per day; actual heart rate changes with activity and other conditions.
fact_ref_muscular_2_question: Can a muscle produce force without visibly shortening?
fact_ref_muscular_2_text: Yes. During an isometric contraction, muscle tension develops without an overall change in muscle length or joint position. Holding an object still requires force even when there is no visible movement.
fact_ref_circulatory_0_question: Why are capillary walls much thinner than arterial walls?
fact_ref_circulatory_0_text: Arteries carry blood under pressure and have substantial supporting walls. Capillaries have very thin walls that support exchange with tissues. Their short diffusion distance helps substances move between blood and surrounding tissues.
fact_ref_circulatory_1_question: How can heart rate and blood volume per beat tell you flow per minute?
fact_ref_circulatory_1_text: Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. For example, 70 beats per minute × 70 mL per beat = 4.9 L per minute. This is an illustrative calculation, not a fixed value for every person.
fact_ref_circulatory_2_question: Why must the body keep making red blood cells?
fact_ref_circulatory_2_text: Red blood cells wear out and are removed, while red bone marrow produces replacements. About 120 days is a typical lifespan estimate, not an exact lifetime for every red cell.
fact_ref_nervous_0_question: Are neurons the only cells that help the nervous system work?
fact_ref_nervous_0_text: Neurons communicate through electrical and chemical signals. Glial cells also matter: they support neurons, regulate their surroundings, and in some cases form myelin. Different cell types work together within neural circuits.
fact_ref_nervous_1_question: Do all nerve signals travel at the same speed?
fact_ref_nervous_1_text: Conduction speed varies with properties such as axon diameter and myelination. In myelinated axons, action potentials are regenerated at gaps called nodes of Ranvier. One maximum speed does not describe every nerve fiber.
fact_ref_nervous_2_question: Why do neurons need energy even between signals?
fact_ref_nervous_2_text: Neurons maintain unequal ion concentrations across their membranes. ATP-powered pumps help maintain these gradients, which make electrical signaling possible. Metabolic energy use is different from electricity delivered by a battery to a light bulb.
fact_ref_lymphatic_0_question: Do lymph nodes and the spleen filter the same fluid?
fact_ref_lymphatic_0_text: Lymph nodes filter lymph and bring it into contact with immune cells. The spleen monitors blood. Both support immune defense, but their fluid pathways differ.
fact_ref_lymphatic_1_question: What does the spleen do with aging red blood cells?
fact_ref_lymphatic_1_text: The spleen helps remove old or damaged red blood cells and supports immune responses to material in the blood. Components of the removed cells can be recycled.
fact_ref_lymphatic_2_question: How can lymph move without a central pump like the heart?
fact_ref_lymphatic_2_text: Lymph flow is helped by body movement, breathing-related pressure changes, and contractions of lymphatic vessel walls. Valves limit backward flow as fluid returns toward the venous circulation.
fact_ref_organs_0_question: Is the liver's only job to remove harmful substances?
fact_ref_organs_0_text: The liver processes nutrients, makes important blood proteins, produces bile, and transforms many substances. Many of these functions occur at the same time.
fact_ref_organs_1_question: How can the small intestine increase contact with digested nutrients?
fact_ref_organs_1_text: Circular folds, villi, and microscopic microvilli increase the small intestine's absorptive surface. A fold, a villus, and a microvillus are different levels of this structure.
fact_ref_organs_2_question: Why is the volume of kidney filtrate much greater than the volume of urine?
fact_ref_organs_2_text: An adult reference estimate is about 180 L of filtrate per day. Kidney tubules return most filtered water and many useful solutes to the blood. Only a small fraction of the filtered fluid becomes urine.
fact_ref_integumentary_0_question: How does the epidermis receive nutrients if it has no blood vessels?
fact_ref_integumentary_0_text: Nutrients diffuse to the epidermis from blood vessels in the underlying dermis. Skin has multiple layers with different structures; the outer layer does not contain its own blood vessels.
fact_ref_integumentary_1_question: Does the entire skin replace itself on one fixed schedule?
fact_ref_integumentary_1_text: Cells formed in deeper epidermal layers move toward the surface and are eventually shed. Renewal is gradual, and timing varies. The whole skin, including its dermis, does not all become new at once.
fact_ref_integumentary_2_question: Why can skin stretch and then partly recover its shape?
fact_ref_integumentary_2_text: Dermal collagen helps resist pulling, and elastic fibers help skin recoil. Stretching has limits: these tissues can be injured, and recovery depends on factors such as age and the extent of damage.
fact_ref_respiratory_0_question: How do breathing rate and breath size determine air moved per minute?
fact_ref_respiratory_0_text: Minute ventilation equals breathing rate × tidal volume. For example, 12 breaths per minute × 0.5 L per breath = 6 L per minute. Some inhaled air stays in conducting airways, so not all of it reaches gas-exchange surfaces.
fact_ref_respiratory_1_question: Why do many small alveoli help gas exchange?
fact_ref_respiratory_1_text: Alveoli provide a large surface with a thin barrier between air and blood. Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse down their own partial-pressure gradients; air does not normally flow directly into blood vessels.
fact_ref_respiratory_2_question: What pushes air out during a quiet breath?
fact_ref_respiratory_2_text: After inspiratory muscles relax, elastic recoil helps reduce lung volume and raise alveolar pressure above atmospheric pressure. Quiet exhalation is mainly passive; forceful exhalation recruits additional muscles.
fact_ref_endocrine_0_question: Does the pituitary directly control every endocrine gland?
fact_ref_endocrine_0_text: The hypothalamus and pituitary regulate many endocrine pathways, but not every hormonal response starts there. Pancreatic islet cells, for example, respond to changes in blood nutrients as well as other signals.
fact_ref_endocrine_1_question: Do adrenaline and cortisol come from the same part of the adrenal gland?
fact_ref_endocrine_1_text: The adrenal medulla releases catecholamines such as adrenaline. The outer adrenal cortex produces steroid hormones, including cortisol. Different tissues and signals contribute to the body's stress response.
fact_ref_endocrine_2_question: Does the endocrine pancreas release only insulin?
fact_ref_endocrine_2_text: Pancreatic islets contain several cell types. Beta cells release insulin, and alpha cells release glucagon. These hormones have different effects that contribute to regulating blood glucose.
fact_ref_reproductive_0_question: Is an ovarian follicle the same thing as an egg cell?
fact_ref_reproductive_0_text: An ovarian follicle contains an oocyte and surrounding supporting cells. The follicle and the oocyte are different structures, and their sizes change during development.
fact_ref_reproductive_1_question: Why does a sperm cell have a head and a long tail?
fact_ref_reproductive_1_text: The sperm head contains the nucleus and an acrosome that contributes to fertilization. Its flagellum supports movement. Comparing cell sizes requires specifying length, width, or volume.
fact_ref_reproductive_2_question: Does placental exchange require maternal and fetal blood to mix directly?
fact_ref_reproductive_2_text: Maternal and fetal circulations normally remain separate, with exchange across placental tissues. Oxygen and nutrients pass toward the fetus, while carbon dioxide and other wastes pass toward the maternal circulation.
fact_ref_heart_g35: The heart has four chambers. It contracts to pump blood and relaxes to fill again. Its rate changes, for example when you exercise or rest.
fact_ref_femur_k2: The femur is your thigh bone. It helps support you when you stand and move.
fact_ref_femur_g35: The femur is the long bone in your thigh. It joins the hip and knee and helps support your body during movement.

notes_ref_femur_clinical: A femoral-neck fracture can damage vessels supplying the femoral head, increasing the risk of bone injury from reduced blood flow. Risk and recovery depend on fracture pattern, displacement, treatment, and the person's health; one mortality percentage is not a prognosis for an individual.
notes_ref_femur_prompt: How could a fracture near a bone's blood supply affect tissue beyond the break?
notes_ref_quads_clinical: The quadriceps tendon and patellar tendon transmit force through the knee's extensor mechanism. A complete tendon rupture can prevent active knee extension. Anterior knee pain alone does not establish a tendon rupture or a single-muscle cause.
notes_ref_quads_prompt: Trace the force from quadriceps muscle to tibia. What changes if a tendon in that chain is disrupted?
notes_ref_rotator_cuff_clinical: Rotator-cuff tendons help transmit muscle force and stabilize the shoulder. A tear may produce pain or weakness, but pain with arm elevation is not specific to a tear. History, examination, and appropriate imaging are interpreted together.
notes_ref_rotator_cuff_prompt: Why should pain-limited movement be distinguished from weakness when interpreting shoulder function?
notes_ref_aorta_clinical: An aortic aneurysm is an abnormal enlargement; a dissection separates layers of the aortic wall. Repair decisions depend on the affected segment, size, growth, symptoms, and patient factors. A single diameter cutoff does not apply to every aneurysm. Suspected acute dissection is an emergency.
notes_ref_aorta_prompt: Why do the location and condition of a vessel wall matter in addition to its diameter?
notes_ref_carotid_clinical: Carotid plaque can narrow the artery or release material that obstructs vessels supplying the brain. Stenosis can increase stroke risk, but does not mean a stroke has occurred. Decisions about intervention depend on symptoms, severity, expected benefit, and procedural risk, rather than a percentage alone.
notes_ref_carotid_prompt: How could material from a neck artery affect a smaller vessel inside the brain?
notes_ref_hippocampus_clinical: Hippocampal injury can impair formation of new memories. Reduced hippocampal volume may occur in several conditions; MRI shrinkage alone does not establish Alzheimer's disease. Clinical history, cognitive assessment, and other appropriate investigations help interpret an imaging finding.
notes_ref_hippocampus_fn: The hippocampus is part of a medial temporal network involved in forming new episodic memories and representing spatial relationships. Memory depends on interacting brain regions and several distinct processes, rather than a single transfer from short-term to long-term storage.
notes_ref_hippocampus_detail: Brain structure, function, and behavior provide different kinds of evidence. An association between hippocampal volume and a symptom does not, by itself, establish the cause of that symptom.
notes_ref_hippocampus_prompt: What is the difference between observing a smaller structure and identifying the cause of that change?
notes_ref_spleen_clinical: The spleen is richly supplied with blood, so traumatic injury can cause serious bleeding. Some stable patients can be managed with monitoring and sometimes embolization, while others need surgery. Management depends on circulation, injury findings, and available expertise; injury does not automatically mean splenectomy.
notes_ref_spleen_clinicalKid: Your spleen helps clean the blood by removing old blood cells. It also helps immune cells respond to germs in the blood. Different parts of the spleen do these related jobs.
notes_ref_spleen_prompt: Why would a patient's circulation and bleeding change the response to injury in a blood-rich organ?
notes_ref_kidneys_clinical: Kidney disease can disrupt filtration, fluid balance, electrolytes, and acid-base regulation. Dialysis is started using a combined assessment of symptoms, signs, laboratory findings, kidney function, and the person's preferences. A low filtration estimate alone is not an automatic start rule.
notes_ref_kidneys_prompt: Why might two people with similar filtration estimates have different needs for dialysis?
notes_ref_pancreas_clinical: Pancreatic disease can affect enzyme-producing tissue, ducts, or endocrine cells. In pancreatic cancer, outlook and treatment depend on cancer type, extent, resectability, and the person's health. A single survival percentage cannot describe every pancreatic tumor or predict an individual's outcome.
notes_ref_pancreas_prompt: Why would the cell type and extent of a tumor matter when interpreting disease in one organ?
notes_ref_sweat_glands_clinical: Sweat evaporation helps remove heat, but cooling also depends on conditions such as humidity and airflow. Heat stroke can occur with dry skin or profuse sweating. Sweating does not rule it out; suspected heat stroke with altered mental status is an emergency.
notes_ref_sweat_glands_prompt: Why does producing sweat not guarantee that enough heat is leaving the body?
notes_ref_testes_repro_clinical: Testicular torsion twists the spermatic cord and can compromise blood flow. Sudden severe testicular pain requires urgent assessment. Tissue injury risk rises with delay, but a fixed hour limit must not be used to postpone care or assume that assessment is no longer worthwhile.
notes_ref_testes_repro_prompt: How can twisting a cord threaten tissue supplied by vessels inside it?
notes_ref_epididymis_clinical: Epididymal inflammation can cause scrotal pain and swelling, which can overlap with testicular torsion. Pain relief when the scrotum is elevated must not be used by itself to exclude torsion. Sudden severe pain or an uncertain diagnosis needs urgent clinical assessment.
notes_ref_epididymis_prompt: Why is a change in pain with position insufficient to prove that blood flow is safe?
notes_ref_prostate_clinical: Benign prostate enlargement can affect urine flow because the gland surrounds the urethra. PSA can rise with cancer and with noncancerous conditions. An elevated PSA or an examination finding prompts interpretation and further evaluation; neither alone confirms prostate cancer.
notes_ref_prostate_prompt: How can a marker come from one organ without identifying one specific disease?

spot_ref_legs: in the lower body, around the legs
spot_ref_left: on the left side of the figure
spot_ref_right: on the right side of the figure
spot_ref_center: near the center of the figure
spot_ref_need_four: Spotter needs at least four different structures in view. Choose another view or enable more layers.
spot_ref_intro: Identify the structure at the crosshair. Take time to compare the choices, then use the feedback to review its function.
spot_ref_timing_help: Untimed practice is the default. Timing is a personal challenge; it does not change answer credit or measure mastery. There is no time limit.
spot_ref_viewer: Left and right refer to the viewer. The cue locates the marker, not the full extent of the structure.
spot_ref_incomplete: This saved Spotter round is incomplete.
spot_ref_fresh_help: Start a fresh round using structures visible in the current diagram.
spot_ref_hidden: The marked structure is hidden by the current view or layer filters.
spot_ref_hidden_help: Restore its view or layer to see the crosshair. You can still use the position cue, or choose a visible structure.
spot_ref_pick_visible: Pick a structure in this view
spot_ref_read_feedback: Read the marked structure explanation aloud
camera_refit_done: View refitted. Your viewing angle is unchanged.
surface_canvas_compact: Interactive external body surface. Choose a body region, drag or open Rotate & tilt to rotate, and use plus or minus to zoom. Refit view keeps your current region and angle. Reset, Home, or R returns to the whole body. Explore structure pins in Blueprint or the 2D Atlas.
surface_controls_compact: Choose a body region above. Open Rotate & tilt for camera buttons, or drag to inspect the body. Zoom, Refit view, and Reset are below the model. Refit preserves your region and angle; Reset returns to the whole body. Soft and Contour change the lighting. Use Blueprint or the 2D Atlas for labeled structures and internal organs.
region_intro: Start with these structures. Blueprint shows their location; Read opens the full explanation.
region_opened: {structure} selected in Blueprint. Use Read to open its explanation.
region_reading_intro: Read more here without leaving the model, or open a structure in Blueprint to locate it.
region_return_done: Your previous body view is restored.
